messages.author: 1e1f02e079119aa4
messages.subject: spatial models
parts:
Rather than assuming that all of my sites are completely (and identically) "independent", I'm wondering if it would be possible to incorporate the Euclidian distances between each pair into the analysis.  So then the assumption would be that the "independence" of any two sites is a linear function of the distance between them.  I don't know much about this (obviously), but my impression is that this is how phylogenetic comparative methods work -the independence of two species is a function of the phylogenetic distance between them.

Would it be possible to do this in a pcount or occu model by doing something like fixing the covariance matrix to be a matrix of the geographic distances between each pair of sites? 

I saw a few threads related to assessing spatial dependence of model residuals post-hoc, but couldn't find anything about incorporating spatial effects explicitly into the models.  But I apologize if I've missed earlier discussions of this!

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] spatial models
parts:
hi Jaya,
 The functions in unmarked currently do not allow for including spatial process models except as defined by explicit covariates (e.g., polynomials of space).  There are now several examples here and there in the literature of both N-mixture and occupancy models that include certain types of spatial models.
regards
andy

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] spatial models
parts:
Dear all,

you can find code in the literature on how to fit CAR spatial random effects into occupancy or Nmix models using WinBUGS and OpenBUGS. There are also a couple of R packages that allow you to fit static occupancy models with CAR or related spatial processes:
- stocc: CAR and so-called restricted spatial regression; does static occupancy using Bayesian MCMC
- hSDM: does CAR for static occupancy using MCMC (but does not call the model an occupancy model; one of them is exactly a static occupancy model)
- Paul Conn has written an R package to do hierarchical distance sampling with CAR priors, I believe. Can't remember the name now.

Plus, there must be a couple of others. The trouble is that most spatial statisticians don't go into the field ever and so are not aware of the benefits of adding a model component for imperfect detection (i.e., there will be lots of packages that allow you to fit spatial models to relative occurrence and relative abundance).

Kind regards  --  Marc
